title: Advantages and disadvantages of the market system

blocks.heading: What this section asks you to do
blocks.text: Explain the advantages and disadvantages of the market economic system, with examples from different countries, and weigh the two sides for named groups.

blocks.heading: How the machinery produces its advantages
blocks.text: Prices act as signals and incentives. When mangoes at the Oshakati open market are scarce after a poor harvest, the price rises; the higher price tells buyers to take less and tells any farmer with fruit that bringing it is now worth the trip, so resources move to the good people want most. The same chain drives consumer sovereignty: Kaoko Juice earns revenue where buyers spend, so it tends to produce the flavours buyers choose. Competition adds a third advantage: a seller charging far above its rivals tends to lose sales, so rivalry holds prices down and choice wide. Together the profit motive and prices move resources to their most valued uses without a central plan. Vietnam's farm markets after its 1980s reforms show the same chains at work.

blocks.heading: Consumer sovereignty, efficiency and innovation
blocks.text:
Three advantages deserve a closer look. Consumer sovereignty means that consumers, through what they choose to buy, decide what is produced. Every N$ spent works like a vote: when shoppers in Ongwediva buy more chicken and less beef, butchers there stock more chicken, because that is where the sales are. No official has to decide what people want; the spending pattern tells firms directly.

The profit motive also pushes firms towards efficiency. A bakery that wastes flour or runs its ovens half-empty has higher costs than its rivals, so it either earns less profit or must charge more and lose customers. Each firm therefore has a reason to produce at the lowest cost it can, which means fewer resources are used up for each loaf.

The same motive drives innovation. A firm that offers a new product or a better method can earn extra profit until rivals catch up, so firms tend to invest in new ideas. Mobile phone banking spread quickly across East Africa once firms saw the profit in serving people without bank accounts, and in South Korea competing electronics makers have long raced to bring out new models. The advantage depends on rivalry being real: a firm that faces no competitor feels far less pressure to cut costs or to innovate.

blocks.heading: Where the machinery misfires
blocks.text: The market system also misfires. Income is distributed unevenly, because rewards follow scarce skills and ownership: a household owning two taxis earns far more than a security guard. Street lighting in Katutura tends to be under-provided, because a firm cannot charge each person who benefits from the glow. Goods that impose costs on others may still be produced where the profit is good: a plant releasing waste into a river keeps the sales while people downstream carry the harm. And work is not guaranteed, because firms hire for expected profit, not for the need for jobs.

blocks.heading: Monopoly power and resources left idle
blocks.text:
Two further disadvantages arise from how real markets work. The first is the abuse of monopoly power. Competition protects consumers only where rivals exist. Where one firm, or a handful, controls a market - the only cement supplier in a region, or the only bus company on a route - it may raise its price, hold back output or let quality slip, because buyers have nowhere else to go. Consumers then pay more for less, and the advantage of competition is lost.

The second is that the market does not move resources smoothly when demand changes. When demand for a product falls, the firms that make it cut output and shed workers. In principle those workers move to industries where demand is growing, but factors of production are often immobile: a miner in Tsumeb may lack the skills for a hotel job and may be unable to move to the coast where the hotels are. Machines and buildings designed for one product may have no other use. So unemployment and idle capital can last for years in one area while other areas are short of workers. The market system offers no automatic guarantee that every worker who wants a job will find one.

blocks.heading: Market systems in different countries
blocks.text: No country runs a pure market system, but countries lean on it to different degrees. The United States relies heavily on private firms and prices: most health care is bought from private providers, and incomes are more unequal than in most other rich countries. Germany calls its approach a social market economy: private firms and free prices run most of the economy, but the state provides wide social insurance, so the market's disadvantages are cushioned. Vietnam shows a country moving towards the market. From the late 1980s it let farmers sell their crops at market prices and keep the proceeds, and rice output rose fast enough to turn the country into a major rice exporter - the price incentive at work - although income gaps widened as some regions and households gained more than others. Namibia's own economy is mixed: private firms, from Oshakati market traders to large mining companies, make most production decisions, while the state runs some services and firms itself. The comparison shows that the advantages and disadvantages in this topic appear in every country that uses markets, and that countries differ mainly in how far they let the market decide.

blocks.heading: Weighing the two sides
blocks.text: The judgement depends on the good and the group. For consumer goods - juice, clothing, haircuts - the market's advantages dominate: choice is wide, rivalry holds prices down, resources follow what buyers value. For goods that spread their benefits beyond the buyer, or for households with no resources to sell, the disadvantages bite hardest. The weighing ends with a condition: the market serves consumers well where goods can be sold one-by-one and rivalry is real. Topic 2.11 shows the compromise most countries adopt.

blocks.heading: Connections
blocks.text: The misfires named here are gathered up as market failure in topic 2.10; the responses a government can make belong to topic 2.11; the rivalry that holds prices down reappears in topic 3.8.
